tools.name: run_monte_carlo_simulation
tools.title: Run a Monte Carlo simulation of a model
tools.description: Runs a Monte Carlo simulation of a model and returns the full range of possible outcomes, not one guessed number. A model is a set of uncertain inputs, the formulas that combine them, and the links between them. The simulation draws random values for every input many times; each draw is a trial, and one call is one run. Use this when you need to know how likely different outcomes are for a plan built on uncertain inputs. It returns, for every node and time period, the mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, 10th to 90th percentiles (the value a given share of trials fall below) and a histogram. It also returns any financial metrics you asked for, such as NPV or IRR, and a run_id. The run finishes within this call, so there is nothing to poll. Cost: without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day (models up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes); with an account, 1 credit for a small run or 5 for a large one, currently $0.50 per credit. A model that is invalid or over the no-account limits is rejected before running and costs nothing. If it fails mid-run: anonymous, the free run is used; account, not charged.

AggregationRequest.description: A financial metric computed over one node's whole time series in every trial, then summarized as a distribution. Available: npv (net present value), irr (internal rate of return), mirr (modified IRR), payback and discounted_payback (periods until cumulative cash turns positive), cagr (compound annual growth rate), cumsum (running total), terminal_value, and prob (the chance a value passes a threshold). Discounting counts periods from 0: the first period is not discounted. Model an up-front investment as a negative value in period 0. Do not also discount inside the node's formula with PV() or DISCOUNT(), which count from 1, or the first period is discounted twice. cumsum gives one number per trial: the total of the node's values over every simulated period. output_request.time_periods does not shorten it. prob can target any earlier metric, including npv and cumsum. Its mean in the result is the probability, the share of trials that pass. A prob that targets a node directly only tests the node's final-period value. Recipe for the chance that a cumulative total over the first N periods beats X: add {id: total, function: cumsum, target_node_id: <node>}, then {id: p, function: prob, target_aggregation_id: total, params: {op: '>', value: X}}, and read aggregations.p.basic_stats.mean. This works directly when the model has exactly N periods. If it has more, point cumsum at a calc node with formula IF({time_period} <= N, {e1}, 0). {time_period} counts from 1. Use cumsum and prob for totals and probabilities here. A running-total node is needed only for rank_inputs_by_impact and summarize_outcome_scenarios, which measure one node in one period.

tools.name: rank_inputs_by_impact
tools.title: Rank which inputs drive an outcome most (one-at-a-time sensitivity)
tools.description: Ranks a model's uncertain inputs by how much each one moves a chosen outcome, and returns the data for a tornado chart. A tornado chart is a bar chart with one horizontal bar per input, sorted with the biggest swing at the top. This is a one-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity analysis. Every input is held at its median while one input at a time is set to low, middle and high values from its own distribution (by default its 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles). The tool records how the outcome's average changes. Use this when you need to know which assumption matters most, so you know what to research or de-risk first. It returns one entry per input, ranked so rank 1 has the biggest impact. Each entry lists the input values tried, the outcome at each, and an elasticity score. Elasticity means how strongly the outcome reacts: roughly, how many percent the outcome moves when the input moves 1 percent. It returns numbers, not an image, and no run_id, so get_simulation_results cannot fetch it later. Inputs whose distribution produces a list of values are skipped. Cost: without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day for each call, even though the analysis runs the model many times (models up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes); with an account, 1 credit for a small model or 5 for a large one, currently $0.50 per credit. A model that is invalid or over the no-account limits is rejected before running and costs nothing. If it fails mid-run: anonymous, the free run is used; account, already charged, because this tool charges when the analysis starts.

tools.description: Runs a model once and reports one outcome's worst, median and best values. By default, worst is the lowest value in any trial, median is the middle value, and best is the highest value. Worst always means lowest, so for a cost the worst case is the cheapest one. You can ask for other percentiles instead, such as the 10th and 90th. Use this when you want a short worst, typical and best case story rather than the full distribution. For the full distribution, use run_monte_carlo_simulation. To find which input matters most, use rank_inputs_by_impact. It returns each scenario's outcome value and every input's own value at the same percentile. Those input values are an estimate, not the exact inputs of that trial. It returns no run_id, so get_simulation_results cannot fetch it later. Cost: without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day (models up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes); with an account, 1 credit for a small run or 5 for a large one, currently $0.50 per credit. A model that is invalid or over the no-account limits is rejected before running and costs nothing. If it fails mid-run: anonymous, the free run is used; account, not charged.

tools.name: convert_range_to_distribution
tools.title: Turn a min–max guess into distribution parameters
tools.description: Turns a low-to-high guess, such as "between 80 and 120, 90% sure", into the exact parameters a model input needs. A distribution is the shape of the uncertainty, for example normal (a bell curve), log_normal (skewed and never negative), triangle or uniform. The low and high values are the edges of the range you are that sure of, not hard limits. Use this when you have a rough estimate and need distribution parameters instead of guessing them. Its reverse is convert_distribution_to_range. It returns the distribution type and its parameters, ready to use as a model input's distribution_params. The distribution_type parameter explains which type fits which kind of quantity. Supported types: normal, log_normal, uniform, triangle, beta, gamma, exponential, binomial, discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal, discrete_gamma, constant and bernoulli. Not supported: poisson, categorical, dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array. For beta, give low and high as fractions (2% is 0.02). Cost: free; uses no credits and no free runs.

distribution_type.description: The distribution to fit. Which to pick: a rate or proportion between 0 and 1 (conversion, churn) → beta, with low and high given as fractions (2% is 0.02). A positive amount that can run high (revenue, price, deal size) → log_normal. A quantity equally likely to land above or below its middle → normal. A value with hard limits you know → uniform (flat) or triangle (most likely value in between). A whole-number count (customers, units) → discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal or discrete_gamma, or binomial for successes out of a fixed number of attempts. Not supported here: poisson, categorical, dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array.
distribution_type.title: Distribution Type

min_estimate.description: The low end of your range. Required for every type except constant and bernoulli. Exponential ignores it, but a value must still be sent (any number works).
min_estimate.title: Min Estimate

max_estimate.description: The high end of your range. Required for every type except constant and bernoulli.
max_estimate.title: Max Estimate

percentile_range.description: A single fraction: the share of outcomes that should fall between the low and high ends, which is how sure you are. The default 0.9 means the middle 90%: a 5% chance of being below the low end and 5% above the high end. Mapping hedged words: "very sure" or "almost certainly" is about 0.9; "probably" is about 0.8; if unsure, ask the user. "Could be higher" means pick a right-skewed type such as log_normal, not a wider range.
percentile_range.title: Percentile Range

mode_estimate.description: The most likely value. Required for constant (the fixed value), bernoulli (the chance of success, from 0 to 1) and binomial. For triangle it sets the peak; it must lie strictly between low and high, and defaults to their midpoint. For beta it is used as the peak when a fit allows, but the low and high ends take priority. Ignored by other types.

tools.name: convert_distribution_to_range
tools.title: Turn distribution parameters into a min–max range
tools.description: Turns a distribution's parameters into the low and high ends of the range that holds a chosen share of outcomes, by default the middle 90%. It also gives the mean, median, mode, standard deviation and any percentiles you ask for. If you give a threshold, it gives the chance of landing below and above it. Use this when you have distribution parameters, from a model or from fermi (a companion forecasting server from Kromatic, the company behind Neumann, whose estimates carry next_steps.simulate.root_node), and want to know what they mean in plain numbers. Its reverse is convert_range_to_distribution, and the range it returns can be passed straight back to it. Values that do not apply, such as a uniform distribution's mode, come back as null with a note explaining why. Cost: free; uses no credits and no free runs.

distribution_type.description: The distribution's name. Accepts every type a model input accepts: normal, log_normal, uniform, triangle, beta (values are fractions from 0 to 1), gamma, exponential, poisson, bernoulli, binomial, categorical, constant, discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal and discrete_gamma. categorical returns no range. dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array produce lists of values, so every number comes back null. This is wider than convert_range_to_distribution, which cannot fit poisson or categorical.
distribution_type.title: Distribution Type

distribution_params.description: The distribution's parameters, in the same form a model input uses, for example {"mean": 100, "std": 15} for normal or {"mu": 9.2, "sigma": 0.6} for log_normal.

percentile_range.description: A single fraction: the share of outcomes the returned range should hold, centred on the median. The default 0.9 means the middle 90%, so the range runs from the 5th to the 95th percentile.

quantiles.description: A list of percentiles to report. Each is a fraction from 0 to 1: 0.05 is the 5th percentile, the value 5% of outcomes fall below. No repeats. Default [0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.95], returned under keys p5, p10, p50, p90 and p95.

threshold.description: Optional value to compare against. The result gives the chance of being at or below it and the chance of being above it. For whole-number distributions it gives the chance of being below and above it, and notes the chance of landing exactly on it.
